front.title: Deterministic ECDSA on P-256 with SHA-256

abstract.t: A profile of RFC 6979 for the ECDSA functions of nish/crypto/p256: deterministic ECDSA on NIST P-256, with SHA-256 for the message and HMAC-SHA-256 for the nonce, and the public key computed from the private key. Every requirement quotes RFC 6979, the main source; every binding sentence of RFC 6979 (MUST, MUST NOT, SHALL, SHALL NOT, REQUIRED) is tested or excluded here.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

nish/crypto/p256 signs with ECDSA on P-256 (RFC 6979 Section A.2.5's curve) and draws the nonce k by RFC 6979 Section 3.2 with HMAC-SHA-256. The private key x is 32 big-endian octets, taken as a Secret; the properties see it as bytes. The public key U = xG is the 65-octet uncompressed point, 04, then Ux and Uy as 32 big-endian octets each. A signature is the 64 octets r, then s, each 32 big-endian octets. p256Sign and p256Verify take the message's hash; p256SignSha256 and p256VerifySha256 take the message and hash it with SHA-256. Key generation and signing return u8[] | null, null for a private key outside [1, q-1]; verification returns a boolean.
Out of scope: p256Ecdh, Diffie-Hellman on P-256 (SEC 1 Section 3.3.1), which RFC 6979 does not describe

Out of scope: p256SignSha256Into, the same signature as p256SignSha256 written into a caller's array through a P256SignScratch, held by tests/link/crypto_p256; its message is a (msg, off, len) /* window */ and its (out, at) an /* out 64 */ write, but its first parameter is the class P256SignScratch, which vector 0.6.0 refuses in a ts-interface block ("P256SignScratch is not a ts-interface type; use u8[], string, boolean, i8, i16, i32, i64, u8, u16, u32, u64, f64, Secret<u8[]>, u16[], u32[], u64[], each optionally | null"), and it answers a boolean where an /* out CAP */ write returns the end offset
Out of scope: P256SignScratch, the reusable scratch of p256SignSha256Into, a class and not a function
Out of scope: P256_SCALAR_SIZE, an i32 constant a vector or property cannot call; every property draws a 32-octet private key
Out of scope: P256_POINT_SIZE, an i32 constant a vector or property cannot call; P-PUB-FORM holds the 65-octet public key
Out of scope: P256_SIGNATURE_SIZE, an i32 constant a vector or property cannot call; P-SIG-FORM holds the 64-octet signature

section.name: Interface
section.sourcecode: // module: nish/crypto/p256 export const p256PublicKey = (priv: Secret<u8[]>): u8[] | null export const p256Sign = (priv: Secret<u8[]>, digest: u8[]): u8[] | null export const p256Verify = (pub: u8[], digest: u8[], sig: u8[]): boolean export const p256SignSha256 = (priv: Secret<u8[]>, msg: u8[]): u8[] | null export const p256VerifySha256 = (pub: u8[], msg: u8[], sig: u8[]): boolean // module: nish/crypto/sha256 export const sha256 = (data: u8[]): u8[]

blockquote.t: Produced signatures remain fully compatible with plain DSA and ECDSA.
The relevant standards prescribe that x shall not be 0; hence, x is an integer in the range [1, q-1].
For ECDSA, the public key is the curve point: U = xG
if qlen < blen, then the qlen leftmost bits are kept, and subsequent bits are discarded;
otherwise, qlen-blen bits (of value zero) are added to the left of the sequence (i.e., before the input bits in the sequence order).
bits2int is used during signature generation and verification in standard DSA and ECDSA to transform a hash value (computed over the input message) into an integer modulo q.
The message is first processed by H, yielding the value H(m), which is a sequence of bits of length hlen.
The pair (r, s) is the signature.

section.name: Deterministic ECDSA

blockquote.t: Deterministic (EC)DSA is the process of generating an (EC)DSA signature over an input message m by using the standard (EC)DSA signature generation process (discussed in the previous section), except that the value k, instead of being randomly generated, is obtained through the process described in this section.
Here, we use HMAC with the same hash function H as the one used to process the input message prior to signature generation or verification.
The entropy of that additional data SHALL be at least n bits, preferably n+64 bits or more, where n is the target security level.

section.t: Untested: a variant nish does not implement: the nonce is drawn from the private key and the digest alone, with no additional secret data

section.name: Out of Scope
section.t: Section A.2.5 prints ten signatures under one key: the messages "sample" and "test", each with SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512. Only the two SHA-256 signatures are vectors here. The other eight draw k with HMAC over the same hash as the message (Section 3.1.1), and nish's nonce is always HMAC-SHA-256 whatever the digest, so p256Sign cannot give them: no export of nish/crypto/p256 signs with the nonce of SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-384 or SHA-512. Their verification by p256Verify is not a vector either: its digest argument is H(m), which Section A.2.5 does not print, and vector 0.6.0 has no Call literal for a value computed from a printed one (a sha384("sample") argument), so such a row cites nothing for its digest.

For the same reason p256Sign has no vector of its own: its argument is the SHA-256 of "sample" or "test", which RFC 6979 does not print. P-DIGEST holds p256Sign over that digest equal to p256SignSha256 over the message, for every key and message, so the two SHA-256 vectors of p256SignSha256 fix p256Sign's result on those digests. A vector 0.6.0 derived argument (p256Sign(x = c9af…, sha256("sample")), an argument that a reference function computes from a printed value) would cite it directly.
The other curves of Sections A.2.3 to A.2.17, and DSA (Sections A.2.1 and A.2.2), are not implemented.
Three statements of RFC 6979 are not functional and hold no binding keyword, so they are recorded here, not excluded:

li.t: Section 3.2: the internal values V, K and k are not observable. The two SHA-256 vectors fix the signature, and so the nonce, for the printed key.
Section 3.4: a k that gives r = 0 is unsuitable, and the generation loops. Finding a key and message that reach it is as hard as a preimage of the hash, so no vector or property can drive that path.

Section 4: implementations should use defensive measures against side channels. Timing is not observable by a functional test; the constant-time disassembly check holds the P-256 arithmetic through tests/cases/ct_asm_p256.ts, recorded in docs/security/crypto-ecc.md.

section.t: Section A.2.5's public key U = (Ux, Uy) is not a vector, and so neither are the verifications of its two SHA-256 signatures under it. p256PublicKey returns the uncompressed point, the octet 04 then Ux and Uy (SEC 1 Section 2.3.3), and RFC 6979 does not print the 04. Vector 0.6.0 binds every literal of a cited row to a whole printed value, so concat([04], Ux = 60fe…, Uy = 7903…) is refused ("the 1-byte expect.concat[0] is only part of a value printed in RFC §A.2.5"), and a row cannot take its framing octet from a second source: a vector cites one section. A cited row for an encoded point needs a literal a vector can mark as framing, not printed (a [04] that fidelity skips when the interface documents the encoding), or a concat whose parts cite separate sources. P-PUB-FORM holds the form of every public key, and P-ROUNDTRIP and the tamper properties hold that the public key verifies its private key's signatures and no other's.
ECDSA is malleable: when (r, s) verifies, so does (r, q - s). RFC 6979 is silent on it, so no clause here asks p256Verify to refuse the upper s.

section.name: Properties
section.sourcecode: // P-TAMPER-MSG covers R-COMPAT — flipping any one bit of the message makes the signature invalid forall (x: u8[] /* 32..32 */, msg: u8[] /* 1..100 */, bit: i32 /* 0..799 */) => p256VerifySha256(unwrap(p256PublicKey(x)), flipBit(msg, bit), unwrap(p256SignSha256(x, msg))) === false where bit < 8 * msg.length

// P-TAMPER-KEY covers R-COMPAT — a signature does not verify under another private key's public key forall (x: u8[] /* 32..32 */, y: u8[] /* 32..32 */, msg: u8[] /* 0..100 */) => p256VerifySha256(unwrap(p256PublicKey(y)), msg, unwrap(p256SignSha256(x, msg))) === false where x !== y

front.title: Deterministic Usage of the Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) and Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA)

abstract.t: This document defines a deterministic digital signature generation procedure. Such signatures are compatible with standard Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) and Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) digital signatures and can be processed with unmodified verifiers, which need not be aware of the procedure described therein. Deterministic signatures retain the cryptographic security features associated with digital signatures but can be more easily implemented in various environments, since they do not need access to a source of high-quality randomness.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.
